extracted.intended_audience: students and technical/academic writers (mathematics, computer science, engineering) learning to improve exposition and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and exercises for producing clear, well-organized technical and academic prose (term papers, lectures, textbooks), with both high-level principles and concrete composition drills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Write, rewrite, rewrite, rewrite . . . .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision is essential: most writers must labour over and over on their work. Early drafts are like sketches and should often be discarded; be prepared to throw away nearly all of them. Examples: Mozart (exception) vs Beethoven (rewrote repeatedly). Even published works may need correction in later editions (example: Karnaugh's correction to Nils's A* algorithm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain external critique before publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let anything you write be published without having had others critique it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities provide a good environment for feedback; be mindful of timing and of choosing willing readers. Peer review can catch oversights (example: McCarthy/Lifschitz catching an oversight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the material while you write it
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to teach a course on a topic at the time you are writing it up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching forces clarification and prevents 'inflicting ramblings on the world.' It provides immediate feedback and helps shape exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely to sharpen style
rubrics_metrics.description: Read a great deal; it'll sharpen your style and get your critical faculties working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad reading improves taste and exposes writers to different models and techniques to emulate or avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the reader (use 'deemons')
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the reader's primitives; ask constantly 'How is the reader going to misunderstand me here?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize reader-modeling with background 'deemons' that automatically catch errors and flag stylistic problems (e.g., split infinitives should 'light up in red'). These checks must run automatically rather than as a conscious checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the tools beyond pure language: vocabulary, indexes, tables, graphs, typography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use typography to make distinctions (example: typewriter font for logical formulae). Anticipate future interactive media and be open to discovering 'stable points' in new technologies. A good vocabulary is needed but not necessarily a huge list of big words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the material (writing to learn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing reorganizes your internal model and deepens understanding of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing, giving talks, and taking classes provide internal feedback; often the writer writes to teach/understand themself. Keep a pad to note good utterances. The publishing of ideas is an anticlimax compared to the learning process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify to start
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the reader with something straightforward to start off with; simplify first and elaborate later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can be acceptable to 'lie, if it helps' and add correct details later. Use simplified examples to convey most of the truth with less difficulty (80-20 rule). Avoid overly terse generalizations that make reading painful for non-specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recycling unchanged material
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist the temptation to re-use portions of old material verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New context and emphasis typically require substantial rewriting; older material should be reworked since you are likely wiser and a better writer now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for excellence (continuous striving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep shooting for perfection even if you'll never get there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain high standards, be never fully satisfied, and continually seek improvement; cultural quotations and aphorisms support this ethic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence length and variation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for average sentence length ~15–20 words and strong variation in sentence lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary‑Claire's empirical guidance: for samples of 10 sentences on a page, adult writing averages under 20 words per sentence; aim for 9–10 different lengths out of 10 sentences; ideal distribution resembles a bell curve centered around 15–18 words; the difference between shortest and longest in samples varied 17–37 words. Include some short 'punchy' sentences and occasional long sentences (but don't let a very long sentence be your crucial point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic variety and avoid repetitive templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the same sentence construction repeatedly (e.g., adverbial + subject + transitive-verb + object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with similar average length and variation, two writers can look different due to syntactic templates. Learn many constructions to vary rhythm and pacing; study which syntactic usages are unusual so you won't overuse them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tight parallels deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use adjacent sentences with exactly the same structure (tight parallels) to communicate similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tight parallels are effective but apparently underused by some writers; practice constructing parallels where each member is 15–20 words long to build syntactic muscle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic sentences as a high form (use sparingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic sentences are those whose grammatical and physical ends coincide (no adverbials right of predicate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic sentences are a high literary form more common in church or literary prose than in conference papers; they heighten awareness of sentence control. Practice by rewriting non-periodic sentences as periodic, but use them judiciously in technical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis positions in sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: The front and back of a sentence are emphatic positions; restructure sentences to shift emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast sentences to emphasize different points and verify effects by writing variations; 'the middle of a sentence is sort of a slum.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary exercises (Replace / Multiply)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice substituting words and compiling thesaurus entries to expand lexical command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace: in a five-page passage replace at least three words in every sentence with synonyms without changing meaning. Multiply: choose a word and write a thesaurus entry at all diction levels; compare with real thesaurus. Use multiple dictionaries and a good thesaurus; recommended readings: Sidney Landau's Dictionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax exercises (Transform / Build parallels / Periodic / Emphasize / Nonsense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensive syntactic drills to increase syntactic 'muscle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform: take five pages and rewrite every sentence with different syntax but same meaning. Build tight parallels, write periodic sentences/paragraphs/pages, recast sentences to shift emphasis, and write coherent structured nonsense (connectives in place but no meaning) to practise glue and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual labor (copying) as close reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Use manual copying in varied modalities to slow down and deeply read text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy passages by hand, with left/right hands, with pen/pencil/crayon, typewriter/word-processor; copy passages you like/dislike/difficult/easy/from different eras or authors to learn style. Manual copying reconnects hands and brain and supports careful reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frozen sounds (transcription & reading aloud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcribe spoken material and read your writing aloud or have others read it to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcribe 5 minutes of radio news, lecture, dialog, or extemporaneous speech. Read aloud your own writing and have friends/strangers read it. Mut ter aloud while writing to check cadence and tone; form partnerships to read each other's work carefully but limit how much critique you absorb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks on paper (creative physical constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises that force different physical or formal representations to reveal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: compose a paragraph with eyes shut; rewrite conditional sentences as tables; caption a picture in one or two lines that fit exactly. These force attention to form and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance, voice, and tone drills
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice changing stance, voice, and tone to discover and control authorial effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises include: rewrite textbook explanations as personal letters, argue both sides of an issue, hyperbolize, euphemize, obfuscate, pontificate, inject hesitations, strengthen or vitiate paragraphs, and change tone of sarcastic or factual pieces. Techniques borrowed from speech therapy (exaggerate defects) help reveal voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Train detailed sensory and descriptive skills by expanding/contracting and rethinking descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: expand a short paragraph to five pages then reduce again; describe by a single modality (sight/sound/smell/taste/touch); Louis Agassiz's exercise: describe a small object daily for two weeks to sharpen observational acuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same as / Different from (comparison & analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice making similes, analogies, and fine-grained distinctions among similar words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare two unlike things with a simile, choose two similar things and explain differences, invent extended analogies to explain complex concepts to unfamiliar audiences, and differentiate related thesaurus entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice invention and categorization to build idea-generation habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine random words into sentences, categorize random nouns and explain schemes. Learning invention entails recognizing useful disciplinary ideas and leveraging prior forms rather than inventing everything from scratch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion and verse-writing to build compositional muscles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use verse-writing and metric exercises to strengthen sense of rhythm, diction, and compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Versify prose into various meters, write sonnets daily (and discard them), expand metric lines by a foot, and follow prosody rules faithfully; verse-writing trains attention to conventional rhyme and stress for transferable benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precis (reducing and abstracting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice concise reduction and abstracting without changing core meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce passages by fixed percentages (5%, 25%, 50%) without altering meaning; write abstracts of articles/books in no more than ten sentences; recognize that significant reductions may require structural changes while preserving meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly-real tasks (flip/replace/crunch/unpack/define/exemplify/explain/instruct/joke/translate/Ben Franklin/push)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises simulating realistic writing tasks under constraints to improve clarity and adaptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: flip paragraph order, enforce slow or quick pacing, write descriptions with or without adjectives/adverbs, unpack metaphors into plain comparisons, write dictionary definitions and compare to references, exemplify abstract nouns, rewrite instructions for novices, write a joke, translate from a language you don't know using a bilingual dictionary, reconstruct a passage from minimal hints (Ben Franklin's exercise), and practice timed continuous writing ('push'). Try instructions on real friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tropes and rhetorical-figure practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Work through a handlist of rhetorical terms by writing an example for each figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing examples for every rhetorical figure builds awareness of rhetorical techniques (the author notes the exercise may feel shallow but thinking through it yields benefit). Recommended: Richard Lanham's Handlist of Rhetorical Terms.
